sections.title: Lesson 11.1: Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and the Bank Secrecy Act
sections.overview: Money laundering is the process of disguising the origin or intended use of funds tied to criminal or terrorist activity. The Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and USA PATRIOT Act impose detection, reporting, and recordkeeping obligations on broker-dealers, enforced primarily through FinCEN and OFAC under the U.S. Treasury Department.
key_concepts: Pre-9/11 AML focus: concealing the criminal SOURCE of dirty money (e.g., drug trafficking proceeds).
Post-9/11 (USA PATRIOT Act) focus: also concerned with the DESTINATION/USE of funds (e.g., clean money used for terrorism).

Three Stages of Money Laundering: (1) Placement — cash enters the financial system (most detectable stage); (2) Layering — multiple transactions disguise audit trail; (3) Integration — funds reenter economy appearing legitimate.
FinCEN: Bureau of U.S. Treasury (not DOJ); intelligence agency with no direct enforcement arm; collects CTRs and SARs.

Currency Transaction Report (CTR): Filed for currency receipts over $10,000 in a single day; file within 15 days; retain records 5 years; CTRs apply to CURRENCY only, not checks/wires (any currency, not only U.S. dollars).
Structuring: Designing deposits to fall under $10,000 threshold — prohibited.

Suspicious Activity Report (SAR): Filed for transactions of $5,000 or more (alone or in aggregate) that involve illegal funds, evade BSA, lack lawful purpose, or facilitate crime; file within 30 days; retain 5 years; filing must remain CONFIDENTIAL — subject must not be notified.
USA PATRIOT Act wire transfer recordkeeping: required for transfers of $3,000 or more (names/addresses of sender/recipient, amount, financial institution, account number).
AML Compliance Officer: Required by BSA; need not be a registered person; establishes internal compliance and red-flag detection procedures.
Red flags: lack of concern over costs/risks, frequent large currency deposits, many wires to unrelated third parties, excessive journal entries between unrelated accounts, structuring.

OFAC: Treasury division; maintains SDN (Specially Designated Nationals) list; U.S. persons and entities prohibited from doing business with SDNs; check at account opening, during relationship, and periodically.

Customer Identification Program (CIP): Required by USA PATRIOT Act; firms must notify new customers that information is being requested for verification (posted notice, verbal, or on new account form).
rules: Bank Secrecy Act — establishes Treasury as primary AML regulator; requires CTR for currency > $10,000.
USA PATRIOT Act (2001) — requires SARs, CIPs, wire transfer recordkeeping ≥ $3,000, and broader AML focus on terrorism financing.
Penalties for failure to file CTR: up to $500,000 fine and/or 10 years prison.
CTR retention: 5 years from filing; SAR retention: 5 years from filing date.
FINRA Rule 3310 — AML Compliance Program (requires written program, designated officer, training, independent testing).
formulas: CTR threshold: Currency received > $10,000 in a single day = file CTR within 15 days
SAR threshold: Suspicious transaction ≥ $5,000 (alone or aggregate) = file SAR within 30 days
mnemonics: PLI — Placement, Layering, Integration (stages of money laundering, in order).
CTR = Currency, Ten thousand, Reported in 15 days.
SAR = Suspicious, ≥ $5,000, file in 30 days, Secret (confidential).

sections.title: Lesson 11.2: Market Manipulation and Insider Trading
sections.overview: No security is exempt from antifraud provisions. Manipulative practices — designed to deceive market participants or distort prices — are strictly prohibited, as is trading on material nonpublic information. The Insider Trading Act of 1988 dramatically increased penalties for misuse of inside information.
key_concepts: Market Rumors: Spreading false/misleading information (including via social media — Twitter, Reddit, Facebook, chat rooms) to manipulate prices is prohibited.
Pump and Dump: Accumulate shares cheap, spread positive false rumors to inflate price, then sell (dump) at inflated price.
Front Running: Placing personal orders ahead of known pending customer orders (especially block orders) to profit from anticipated price movement.
Churning (Excessive Trading): Trading solely to generate commissions, inconsistent with client objectives, history, or financial ability — breach of fiduciary duty; principal review required.
Marking the Open / Marking the Close: Entering or falsely reporting trades at open or close to manipulate reported opening/closing prices.
Freeriding: Buying and selling securities before payment is made — prohibited in cash and margin accounts; penalty is 90-day account freeze requiring cash up front.
Matching Orders (Painting the Tape): Coordinated buy/sell at same price to create false appearance of volume/activity.
Inside Information: Material nonpublic information — info that would influence price of stock and has not been disseminated to the public.
Insider Trading: ILLEGAL USE of inside information for gain or to avoid loss; mere possession is not illegal — it's the use.

Tipper and Tippee both liable. Four-prong test: (1) info material & nonpublic; (2) tipper owes fiduciary duty; (3) tipper meets personal benefits test; (4) tippee knew or should have known info was confidential.
Information Barrier / Firewall: Required written supervisory procedures restricting flow of material nonpublic information between firm departments.
Contemporaneous Traders: Persons trading opposite side of market at same time as insider; may sue for up to 5 years after violation.
Bounties (Dodd-Frank): Informants may receive 10%–30% of amounts recovered for original information on securities law violations.

Rule 5130 — Restricted Persons (cannot buy common stock IPOs at POP): member firms; employees of member firms; finders/fiduciaries to underwriter (attorneys, accountants); portfolio managers (banks, S&Ls, insurance, investment companies); 10%+ owners of a member firm; immediate family members (parents, in-laws, spouses, siblings, children, anyone receiving material support).
Aunts, uncles, grandparents are NOT immediate family — unless they live in same household or receive material support.
De minimis exemption: Account may purchase IPO if restricted persons own no more than 10% of beneficial interests.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 — original prohibition on insider trading.
Insider Trading and Securities Fraud Enforcement Act of 1988 — increased penalties.
FINRA Rule 5130 — Restrictions on Purchase and Sale of IPO equity securities.

Penalties for Insider Trading: Civil — up to 3x profit gained or loss avoided; Controlling person — greater of $1 million or 3x profit/loss avoided; Criminal — up to $5 million and/or 20 years prison for individuals; Firm — greater of $25 million or 3x damages.
SEC Rule 10b-5 — Employment of Manipulative and Deceptive Devices.
FINRA Rule 5270 — Front Running of Block Transactions; Rule 5320 — Trading Ahead of Customer Orders.
formulas: Insider trading civil penalty (individual) = up to 3 × (profit gained or loss avoided)
Controlling person penalty = greater of $1,000,000 OR 3 × profit/loss avoided
Firm penalty (for failure to supervise) = greater of $25,000,000 OR 3 × damages
Whistleblower bounty = 10% to 30% of amount recovered
mnemonics: FPCMMMF — Front-running, Pump and dump, Churning, Marking open/close, Matching orders, Market rumors, Freeriding (manipulation list).
Restricted persons under 5130 = 'I-FOAM' — Industry employees, Finders/fiduciaries, Owners (10%+), Asset managers/portfolio managers, Member firms (and immediate family).
Insider Trading Penalty 3-3-5-20: 3x profits (civil), $5 million / 20 years (criminal individual).

sections.title: Lesson 11.3: Prohibited Activities — Senior Investors, Improper Use of Assets, Nonregistered Personnel
sections.overview: Beyond market manipulation, the rules prohibit financial exploitation of senior/specified adult clients, improper use of customer funds and securities (including borrowing/lending without authorization), guarantees, and the performance of registered functions by nonregistered employees.
key_concepts: Specified Adult (FINRA Rule 2165): age 65+; OR age 18+ whom member reasonably believes has a mental or physical impairment rendering them unable to protect own interests.

Financial Exploitation: Wrongful or unauthorized taking/use of funds or securities; or any act/omission to gain control through deception, intimidation, or undue influence (includes use of POA, guardianship).

Trusted Contact Person: Firm must make reasonable efforts to obtain name/contact info at account opening or when updating account info; not required for opening — only reasonable efforts required; written disclosure of authorized contact must be provided.

Temporary Hold on Disbursements: Firm MAY (not required) place temporary hold (up to 15 business days, extendable by state regulator) if reasonable belief of financial exploitation; internal review must begin immediately; notification to trusted contact and authorized parties within 2 business days, unless trusted contact is suspected perpetrator.
Improper Use: Any use of customer funds/securities other than as the customer intended; borrowing without consent is indistinguishable from stealing.

Five Permitted Borrowing/Lending Arrangements (Rule 3240): (1) immediate family — no notice/approval; (2) customer in business of lending (bank) — no approval needed; (3) both registered with same firm — firm approval required; (4) personal relationship outside broker-customer — firm approval required; (5) business relationship outside broker-customer — firm approval required.
Firm must have written procedures in place permitting lending arrangements; otherwise prohibited.
Guarantees Prohibited: No firm/IA/RR may guarantee against loss or guarantee a gain.

Sharing in Customer Accounts (Rule 2150): Allowed only with prior written firm approval AND only in proportion to RR's financial contribution to joint account; exception for immediate family — proportionality not required.
Firms cannot have joint accounts with customers.
Immediate Family for Sharing: parents, in-laws, spouses, children, and anyone receiving material financial support (broadly includes anyone living in same residence).
Nonregistered Personnel — PERMITTED: answer general questions, give literature, set appointments, invite to seminars, handle customer money/securities (must be fingerprinted).
Nonregistered Personnel — PROHIBITED: open accounts, solicit trades, conduct securities business, receive commissions.
Passing the SIE alone does NOT make you registered — must also pass a top-off (e.g., Series 7) exam.
rules: FINRA Rule 2165 — Financial Exploitation of Specified Adults (allows temporary holds up to 15 business days).
FINRA Rule 2150 — Improper Use of Customers' Securities or Funds; Prohibition Against Guarantees and Sharing in Accounts.
FINRA Rule 3240 — Borrowing From or Lending to Customers.
FINRA Rule 2040 — Payments to Unregistered Persons (prohibits commission payment to unregistered persons).
formulas: Temporary hold duration: up to 15 business days (state regulator may extend or shorten)
Trusted contact / authorized parties notification: within 2 business days of hold
Sharing in account: RR share % ≤ RR contribution % (except immediate family)
mnemonics: Specified Adult = '65 or unable' (age 65+ OR 18+ with impairment).
Borrow/Lend exceptions = 'FB-RPB' — Family, Bank-customer, Registered same firm, Personal relationship, Business relationship.
Hold = 15 business days; Notify = 2 business days.

sections.title: Lesson 11.4: Communications with the Public
sections.overview: FINRA Rule 2210 governs all member communications, requiring fair dealing, good faith, balanced risk/benefit disclosure, and prohibiting omission of material facts or misleading statements. Communications are categorized as institutional, retail, or correspondence based on audience and volume, each with its own approval and filing requirements.
key_concepts: General Standards (Rule 2210): All communications must be based on fair dealing/good faith; fair and balanced; no false, exaggerated, or misleading statements; no implication past performance will be repeated; tailored to audience.
Three Categories of Communication: Institutional, Retail, Correspondence.

Institutional Communication: Written communications distributed only to institutional investors (other member firms/RRs, banks, S&Ls, insurance companies, registered investment companies, employee benefit plans, government entities, entities with $50M+ assets, persons acting on behalf of institutional investors); excludes internal firm memos.

Retail Communication: Written communications distributed to MORE THAN 25 retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period; requires principal approval before use; must be filed with FINRA — new member firms file 10 days BEFORE use; established firms file within 10 days OF first use.
Correspondence: Written communications to 25 OR FEWER retail investors within any 30-day period; firm decides whether to require pre-approval or train/document post-use review.
If reason to believe institutional communication will be forwarded to retail — treat as retail.
Filing with FINRA ≠ approval — it is a filing process only.
Social Media: Static content (websites, blogs) generally requires principal pre-approval; interactive posts do not require pre-approval but require firm policies and supervision.
Cannot imply regulator approval or endorsement — overly prominent display of regulator logo or 'Approved by SEC' is misleading and prohibited.

TCPA of 1991 (administered by FCC): Cold-calling rules — must identify name, company, phone/address; calls only between 8:00 am and 9:00 pm prospect's local time; must check company AND National Do Not Call Registry (both lists must be no more than 30 days old).
TCPA exemptions: existing business relationship, prior express permission, tax-exempt nonprofit, noncommercial purpose, legitimate debt collection.
Account Statements: At least quarterly; monthly if penny stocks held; must show activity, positions, balances; must advise customer to report discrepancies.

Trade Confirmations (Rule 10b-10): Sent at or before completion of transaction (settlement date); must show trade date, account #, RR ID, BOT/SLD, quantity, description, yield (callable bonds), CUSIP, price, amount, commission (if agent), capacity (agent or principal), net amount.

Holding Customer Mail (Rule 3150): Written customer request required; standard up to 3 months (longer for acceptable reasons like safety, not convenience); firm must verify customer's instructions still apply at reasonable intervals; firm must inform of alternate access methods.
Customer Account Records: Send copy within 30 days of account opening; update within 30 days of any change; verify at least every 36 months.

Regulation S-P: Protects nonpublic personal information (SSN, balances, history, internet cookies); initial privacy notice at relationship inception; annual notice for customers (ongoing); consumers (one-time) get initial only; reasonable opt-out methods required (check boxes, electronic opt-out, toll-free number) — letter writing NOT reasonable; safeguard requirements include encryption and secure systems.

Business Continuity Plan (BCP — FINRA Rule 4370): Must address data backup/recovery, alternate communications with customers/employees/regulators, alternate physical location, customer access to funds; review annually; senior management principal responsible; two emergency contacts to FINRA (both associated; at least one principal/senior management); update within 30 days of changes; disclose BCP to customers at account opening, on website, and by mail on request.
rules: FINRA Rule 2210 — Communications with the Public (three categories, approval, filing).
FINRA Rule 2231 — Customer Account Statements (quarterly minimum).
FINRA Rule 2232 — Customer Confirmations (at/before completion of transaction).
FINRA Rule 3150 — Holding of Customer Mail.
FINRA Rule 3230 — Telemarketing (incorporates TCPA requirements).
FINRA Rule 4370 — Business Continuity Plans and Emergency Contact Information.
FINRA Rule 4512 — Customer Account Information (30-day records, 36-month update).
SEC Rule 10b-10 — Confirmation of Transactions.
Regulation S-P — Privacy of Consumer Financial Information.
Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991 (TCPA) — administered by FCC.
formulas: Retail communication = > 25 retail investors / 30 calendar days
New member filing: 10 days BEFORE first use; Established member: within 10 days OF first use
Account statement frequency: quarterly (monthly if penny stocks)
Cold calls: between 8:00 am and 9:00 pm prospect's local time
Institutional investor threshold: $50 million+ in total assets
Customer account record: send within 30 days; update every 36 months
mnemonics: '25 in 30' rule — over 25 retail in 30 days = Retail; 25 or fewer = Correspondence.
TCPA = 'Talk Calmly Politely Always' — 8 am to 9 pm prospect's time, identify yourself, check DNC.
BCP contacts: '2 contacts, 1 must be principal/senior management'.
Reg S-P: 'Customers get annual; consumers get one-time'.
New firm files BEFORE (10 days prior); Old firm files AFTER (within 10 days of use).
